title: Ezekiel 4:9–17
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to make bread from mixed grains and eat it by weight, with water by measure, during the days he lies on his side (4:9–11). The fuel the LORD first names for baking it would make the bread unclean, picturing Israel eating unclean food among the nations (4:12–13). Ezekiel, a priest, protests that he has never defiled himself, and the LORD allows a different fuel (4:14–15). The LORD explains that he will “break the staff of bread” in Jerusalem, so that the people eat and drink by measure in fear (4:16–17); compare the covenant warning in Leviticus 26:26. The notes explain the sign briefly in its literary setting. Both traditions read the passage as a picture of siege scarcity and exile, and they note that God hears the prophet’s objection and answers it.

verses.text: “Take for yourself also wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt, and put them in one vessel. Make bread of it. According to the number of the days that you will lie on your side, even three hundred ninety days, you shall eat of it.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel is to make bread from wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt, eating it during the three hundred ninety days. Arminian readers see the mixed grains as a picture of scraping together whatever food remains in a siege.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the bread as part of the same acted message, showing scarcity under judgment. Both traditions read the detail as illustrating siege conditions, explained briefly in context rather than turned into a symbol for each grain.

verses.text: Your food which you shall eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels a day. From time to time you shall eat it.
verses.arminianNotes: His food is to be by weight, twenty shekels a day, eaten from time to time. Arminian readers note the small, measured ration, which pictures the hunger the besieged will suffer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the weighing of food as a sign that the LORD’s judgment reaches daily life itself. Shared ground: both traditions read the measured portion soberly, as a realistic picture of rationing in a siege.

verses.text: You shall drink water by measure, the sixth part of a hin. From time to time you shall drink.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel drinks water by measure, a sixth part of a hin, from time to time. Arminian readers see the limited water joining the limited bread, completing the picture of a city cut off from supply.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that water by measure echoes covenant warnings of scarcity. Both traditions read the verse as part of a sober sign, and they do not dwell on the hardship beyond what the text says.

verses.text: You shall eat it as barley cakes, and you shall bake it in their sight with dung that comes out of man.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel to bake the bread in their sight using fuel that would make it unclean. Arminian readers see the shock of the command as intended to make the exiles feel the defilement of exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the instruction as a sign of uncleanness to come, given in full view of the people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse briefly and soberly, as a pointed sign rather than a detail to dwell on.

verses.text: The LORD said, “Even thus will the children of Israel eat their bread unclean, among the nations where I will drive them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD explains that Israel will eat its bread unclean among the nations where he will drive them. Arminian readers see exile bringing God’s people into conditions where keeping ritual purity becomes very hard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scattering among the nations as covenant judgment, compare Hosea 9:3 by reference. Both traditions read the explanation as the key to the sign: exile means living as a defiled people away from the LORD’s land.

verses.text: Then I said, “Ah Lord GOD! Behold, my soul has not been polluted; for from my youth up even until now I have not eaten of that which dies of itself, or is torn of animals. No abominable meat has come into my mouth!”
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel protests, Ah Lord GOD, that he has never polluted himself or eaten forbidden meat. Arminian readers note that the prophet speaks honestly to God, and that his objection is heard and answered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a priest’s conscience shaped by the law, compare Ezekiel 1:3. Shared ground: both traditions read the protest as reverent, not rebellious, and as a model of bringing a troubled conscience before God.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Behold, I have given you cow’s dung for man’s dung, and you shall prepare your bread on it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers by allowing a different fuel for preparing the bread. Arminian readers see God responding to the prophet’s plea, adjusting the sign without changing its message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s condescension to his servant within the purpose he has set. Both traditions read the concession as showing that God hears his servants, while the sign of coming scarcity and defilement still stands.

verses.text: Moreover he said to me, “Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem. They will eat bread by weight, and with fearfulness. They will drink water by measure, and in dismay;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem, so people eat and drink by measure with fear and dismay. Arminian readers see the sign explained: the city’s own food supply will fail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase staff of bread as echoing Leviticus 26:26 by reference, a covenant sanction now coming to pass. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining the sign plainly, as famine under siege.

verses.text: that they may lack bread and water, be dismayed one with another, and pine away in their iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: They will lack bread and water, be dismayed together, and waste away in their iniquity. Arminian readers note that the suffering is linked to the people’s sin, a consequence of persistent unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as God’s just judgment carried through to its end. Both traditions read the line with pastoral sobriety, recognizing that the suffering of a besieged people is grievous even when it is deserved.
